explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, the Pharisees speak up. They say to Jesus, “Look, why are they doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?” (Mark 2:24). The disciples are just picking grain, and somebody still has a question about it. I'd have pretended to admire the scenery and kept moving, because I fold fast when people stare.

The Sadducees don't show up anywhere in this scene, friend. Mark 2:24 says, “So the Pharisees said to Him…” That's who has the question about the grain. I've grabbed the wrong cutter in a dim kitchen before too, so I get it.

The tax collectors aren't in this scene. The verse says, “So the Pharisees said to Him…” (Mark 2:24). The disciples are picking grain, and the Pharisees are the ones who call it out. Somebody always notices, like the one person who counts the cookies on the cooling rack and spots a missing one.

That's it. Jesus says David “…entered the house of God and ate the consecrated bread…” (Mark 2:26). David was Israel's king later on (2 Samuel 5:3), but here he's just a hungry man. Jesus names Abiathar as high priest at the time, so He's pointing at a real moment from Israel's story. Hungry people and bread, baker. I understand that one on a deep level.

No lamb here, friend. Jesus says David “…entered the house of God and ate the consecrated bread…” (Mark 2:26). The lamb isn't in His answer at all. I think the word "consecrated" can make a person reach for the biggest thing they remember, and I've done that with a recipe card.

That's not what Jesus says. He says David “…entered the house of God and ate the consecrated bread…” (Mark 2:26). The fellowship offering never comes up in His answer. I get the pull, since the house of God sounds like the place for something fancy, and I've grabbed the fancier cutter over the right one before. The text just says bread.

True. Jesus says the consecrated bread “…was lawful only for the priests.” (Mark 2:26). So David ate something that was set aside for the priests. That's the very thing Jesus holds up when the Pharisees bring up what's lawful. He's pointing at what was done, and He doesn't hide that it was only for priests.

Not quite, baker. Jesus says the consecrated bread “…was lawful only for the priests.” (Mark 2:26). So the text says it was for the priests alone. David ate it anyway, and Jesus says he gave some to his companions as well.

explanations.answer: The Sabbath was made for man
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus declares, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” (Mark 2:27). He says it right after the story about David. Think of an oven mitt: it was made for my hands, not my hands for the mitt.

explanations.answer: The Sabbath was made for kings
explanations.explanation: Kings aren't in the line. Jesus says, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” (Mark 2:27). David does show up in the story just before it, but the Sabbath isn't made for one person on a throne. It's made for man.

explanations.answer: The Sabbath was made for priests
explanations.explanation: Priests come up in the story, but not here. In Mark 2:26 the bread was lawful only for the priests. Then Jesus declares, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” (Mark 2:27). I can see how the priests stuck in your head, because the bread detail is a big one.

Careful, friend, that one slips by. Jesus doesn't say man was made for the Sabbath. He says, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” (Mark 2:27). The "not" is doing real work in that sentence, and I've lost a whole batch to one small word before.

Right, it's false. Jesus says, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” (Mark 2:27). That "not" settles it. He says the Sabbath was made for man, and He says man wasn't made for the Sabbath. Small word, big difference.

Lord, yes. Jesus says, “Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.” (Mark 2:28). He's talking about Himself with that name. Lord means He has authority over it, even over the Sabbath the Pharisees just asked about. Straight answer, no hedging, and I admire that, because I hedge about a burnt batch for ten minutes.
Not servant, friend. Jesus says, “Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.” (Mark 2:28). He says Lord, and He says it about Himself. That's a big claim to make in a grainfield.

Student isn't the word. Jesus says, “Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.” (Mark 2:28). He says Lord, and that's a different thing from taking notes on the Sabbath. I've been a student of the oven for years and I still get burned.

explanations.answer: If He will heal on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Yes. Mark 3:2 says, “In order to accuse Jesus, they were watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath.” A man with a withered hand is right there, and they're watching Jesus to see what He will do. I think that has to feel like standing under a very bright oven light.

explanations.answer: If He will read from the scroll
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. Mark 3:2 says they “…were watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath.” Nothing about a scroll comes up in this passage. They had their eyes on Jesus and what He would do about the man with the withered hand.

explanations.answer: If He will teach the crowd
explanations.explanation: Teaching isn't what they're watching for. Mark 3:2 says they “…were watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath.” It's the healing they're waiting on. A crowd isn't even mentioned in this scene, just the man and the ones watching.

True. Mark 3:2 says, “In order to accuse Jesus, they were watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath.” The text gives their reason right there. They were watching in order to accuse Him. That's a heavy reason to have your eyes on someone.

Not this time, baker. Mark 3:2 says, “In order to accuse Jesus, they were watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath.” So the text does say why they were watching, and it was to accuse Him. It's a plain line that is easy to skim past.

Silent, yes. Mark 3:4 says, “But they were silent.” Jesus asks a question about doing good or evil, saving life or destroying it, and nobody says a word. I've been in that quiet room before, usually right after I ask who ate the last cookie.
No arguing here. Mark 3:4 says, “But they were silent.” Jesus asks His question and the room goes quiet. I'd have expected somebody to talk, but the text says they didn't.
The text doesn't have them quoting anything. Mark 3:4 says, “But they were silent.” Jesus puts the question to them and no answer comes. A question that gets nothing back can be loud in its own way.

Restored. Mark 3:5 says Jesus told the man, “Stretch out your hand.” Then it says, “So he stretched it out, and it was restored.” The man did what he was told, and his hand was whole. I love that one, baker. My own edges took a miracle to fix, so I know a good restoration when I see one.
No bandage in this scene. Mark 3:5 says, “So he stretched it out, and it was restored.” Jesus told him to stretch out his hand, and that's when it happened. Nothing had to be wrapped up.

Anointed isn't the word here. Mark 3:5 says, “So he stretched it out, and it was restored.” Anointed has a fancy ring, and I've grabbed the fancier cutter over the right one before. Restored is the word, and it came when the man stretched out his hand.

Yes. Mark 3:6 says the Pharisees “…went out and began plotting with the Herodians how they might kill Jesus.” They leave right after the man's hand is restored. This is a heavy moment, and I think it's okay to say that out loud. The text names the Herodians, so that's who we name.

The chief priests aren't named here. Mark 3:6 says the Pharisees went out and began plotting “…with the Herodians…” That's the group the text gives us. It's a hard verse, and I think it helps to keep close to just what it says.
No soldiers are in this verse. Mark 3:6 says the Pharisees went out and began plotting “…with the Herodians…” The text names that group and nobody else. It's a heavy line.

Kill. That's the word in Mark 3:6: they began plotting “…how they might kill Jesus.” A hand was restored, and right after it the plotting begins. The next time you read this story, notice how fast things turn in just one verse.

Trap isn't the word here. Mark 3:6 says they began plotting “…how they might kill Jesus.” Back in Mark 3:2 they were watching in order to accuse Him, but now the plotting is about killing. The text says kill, and it doesn't soften it.
Question is a lot gentler than the text. Mark 3:6 says they began plotting “…how they might kill Jesus.” The verse says kill, and that's where this story's shadow starts to fall.
